Alyssa Bietz

Many women over 40 wake up at 3AM and fall back asleep within minutes. For others, that 3AM wake-up turns into two hours of lying in the dark watching the clock.

That pattern is one of the most common struggles I see as an Adult Sleep Consultant and CBT-I Practitioner.

It doesn't seem to matter whether someone is a busy professional, caregiver, educator, or business owner. 

The experience is the same. Waking in the middle of the night. Lying there exhausted but unable to settle back into sleep. Dreading the moment the clock comes into view.

Clients often describe reorganizing their entire lives around broken sleep. Avoiding travel. 

Canceling plans. Relying on caffeine to get through the day. Spending hours searching for the next supplement, bedtime routine, or sleep hack that might finally work.

The internal dialogue often sounds like this:
"Why does this keep happening?"
 "What if tonight is another bad night?"
 "What if this is just how sleep will be from now on?"

As a CBT-I Practitioner, I know this ongoing pattern is usually about more than the nighttime wake-up itself.

What many women don't realize is that the more attention, worry, and effort gets directed toward sleep, the more the brain begins expecting wakefulness. 

What may have started as occasional hormonal sleep disruption during perimenopause can become a learned pattern that repeats night after night, even after the hormonal disruption settles.

That's why I created this free guide.

Inside, I share five evidence-based strategies that help women respond differently to middle-of-the-night wakefulness, feel calmer when sleep doesn't come immediately, and begin rebuilding confidence in their ability to sleep naturally.

For anyone who has been waking at 3AM for months and is ready for a practical, evidence-based next step, this free guide is available now.

Go here to download the free guide >>> https://pages.alyssabietzcoaching.com/free-guide

I have spent $2,180 on baby sleep in 5 months. The Snoo. The Ferber attempt. Taking Cara Babies. A private consultant. A second consultant. She still wakes every 45 minutes.

This is what happened in the five months between me, her, and every method I bought trying to fix it.

Before she was born I read seven books. I had a binder. I had a system. I had downloaded three sleep-tracking apps. I'd watched fourteen hours of Taking Cara Babies. I felt prepared in a way I had not felt prepared for anything since the LSAT.

Month 1: The first system worked. She slept three-hour stretches. I cried with relief. I texted my best friend "I've cracked it."

Month 2: The system stopped working. She went from three-hour stretches to 90-minute ones overnight. I started doubling down on wake windows. They kept changing. I kept adjusting.

Month 3: I bought the Snoo. $1,495 plus shipping. She loved it for two weeks. Then she screamed in it. I'd put her down, she'd scream, I'd take her out, hold her until she slept, transfer to crib, she'd wake up the moment her back hit the mattress, scream again. Eight times a night.

I tried Ferber for three nights at month three and a half. She cried for 42 minutes the first night. I picked her up and held her and apologized to her sleeping body for an hour. I never tried it again.

Month 4: Taking Cara Babies. $179. I watched the videos at 1 AM, took notes on the back of a Target receipt, and fell asleep during module 3. I bought Precious Little Sleep too. $35. Couldn't bring myself to start.

Month 4.5: The $400 sleep consultant. 30-minute Zoom. I told her my baby was on the breast every 45 minutes. She told me to "be more consistent with the wake windows." I asked her which ones. She said "the right ones." I paid her the $400 because I'd already paid her the $400.

The second consultant was free. A friend of a friend who did this on weekends. She watched a video of my baby's bedtime and said "have you tried sleep training?" I said yes. She said "have you tried it properly?"

Month 5: I stopped buying things. I stopped opening the apps. I stopped tracking wake windows. I stopped reading the books. I stopped pretending the next thing would be the thing. I just held the baby and counted hours.

The pediatrician at the 4-month appointment said "some babies just don't sleep well until 18 months." She said it the same way she might have said "some kids prefer Cheerios to oatmeal." I left and sat in the parking lot for an hour.

I had already tried everything by month 5. The Snoo. Ferber. Cara Babies. Precious Little Sleep. Two consultants. The Hatch. The Owlet. The Nanit. Three wake-window apps. The dream feed. The dream feed at 10. The dream feed at 11. The "no dream feed because it disrupts the circadian rhythm." The contact nap. The stroller walk that worked exactly once and never again.

None of it worked. Because all of it was about finding the right METHOD.

Nobody — not the consultants, not the pediatrician, not the apps, not the books, not the moms in my Facebook group — had ever asked me how I was doing.

I stopped trying. Not dramatically. Just quietly. I stopped saving methods to my bookmarks bar. I stopped joining Facebook groups. I stopped pretending I was going to crack it. I just got through each night and started counting time in 45-minute increments because that's how she divided it.

One Saturday afternoon I caught myself in the Target parking lot googling "is the Lovevery sleep method real?" with the baby asleep in the car seat next to me. I'd googled the same question. Three weeks earlier. Twice. I sat there for ten minutes realizing I had been looking for the same answer for 22 weeks and I was still looking and I had never once looked at myself.

That night I couldn't sleep even with her finally down. 1:45 AM. I scrolled past a comment on a moms forum from a stranger I'll never know. She wrote:

You're not failing. You're drowning. There's a difference. Failing is doing it wrong. Drowning is doing everything right while the water keeps rising around you. They keep trying to fix the baby. Nobody throws a rope to the mom.

I read it four times. Then I cried — a different kind of crying. The kind where something finally lets go in your chest.

I had been buying methods. Five months of methods. Five months of advice that assumed the next method would be the right one. Nobody had told me that the issue wasn't the method. It was the foundation underneath all of them.

Underneath the comment was a link. A 3-minute quiz. I clicked expecting another method calculator. The first question wasn't "which method have you tried?" It said: "How are YOU doing?"

I burst into tears at the question. Nobody had asked me that in five months.

It was called Betteroo. 37,432 moms had taken it before me. Fifteen minutes a day. No cry-it-out. Built around me first — my sleep, my body, my actual life — and then around her. It wasn't another method to add to my collection. It was the thing the methods all assumed I had and didn't.

Week 1: Three slow exhales before walking into the nursery. A glass of water before picking her up. I felt stupid. I almost stopped on day three. The only reason I didn't stop was because the program wasn't asking me to optimize HER. It was asking me to do small things for me, regardless of what she did.

Week 2: I deleted three sleep-tracking apps. I deleted Huckleberry. I cancelled my Taking Cara Babies subscription. I emailed the $400 consultant and asked for the refund she had refused. She did not respond. I felt clearer than I had in months.

Week 3: She slept four hours in the Snoo without me bouncing her. The Snoo wasn't different. She wasn't different. I was different. I had stopped white-knuckling through every wake. I had stopped reading wake windows in my head while she nursed.

Week 4: She slept six hours straight in the Snoo. Six. I woke up confused, thinking I had missed an alarm. Nothing was wrong. She had just slept. And I had too.

My husband walked into the kitchen at 7 AM and found me already up, already making coffee, already smiling. He said: "I haven't seen you smile in a month."

I didn't say anything back. Just made him a cup too.

It's been six weeks. She still wakes at night. I still get tired. The Snoo is still the Snoo. The methods are still the methods. The only thing that changed was me.

If you've spent over a thousand dollars on baby sleep and nothing has worked...
If you have three sleep apps on your phone you check before you check the weather...
If a consultant refused to refund you and you're still telling yourself you'll "find the right method"...
If you've found yourself googling the same question for the third time and not noticed...
If the methods have started to feel like the problem...

It might not be that you haven't found the right method.
It might be that you've been drowning while shopping for life rafts.
And there's a difference.

The link is below. It's a 3-minute quiz. The first question is: "How are YOU doing?"

The second question is "what have you already tried?" — and they actually read the answer.

That's all I needed someone to do.

Take the quiz. 💙

I needed a reset. Not another method.
Get yourself back, not just your child's sleep. A gentle, personalized sleep program that starts with YOU, with real sleep experts in your corner. Take the free 3-minute quiz. No cry-it-out. Over 71,000 exhausted parents have started here.

CPAP "fixed" my sleep apnoea. I still wake up exhausted every morning. My GP told me to persevere. That was 12 months ago.

I need to tell you something I've been too embarrassed to say out loud.

I'm 49. Married 22 years. Two kids. I'm a regional operations manager at a logistics firm in the West Midlands. Been there 14 years.

Twelve months ago I was diagnosed with severe sleep apnoea. AHI of 47. I got a CPAP two months later.

I have been using the machine every night since.

My AHI is 0.4. I wear the mask 8 hours a night. On paper the CPAP is working perfectly.

I've done everything they told me to do.

And I'm writing this at 3:14 AM because I woke up exhausted again - like I do every morning - and no doctor can help me.

Who I Used To Be

I used to be sharp.

I remembered every customer. Every account number. Every quote I'd put in.

I ran the Q3 review from memory. No notes. My deputy took notes.

I coached Jack's football team until he was 14 and grew out of it.

I fixed the boiler when it packed up in February. Fixed the neighbour's boiler the same week.

I read to Sophie every night until she was 11.

I was the man Claire married.

I haven't been that man for about a year now.

And here's the bit I still can't accept.

The CPAP didn't bring him back.

What Started Happening Before The Diagnosis

The snoring got bad a couple of years ago. Claire told me. I didn't notice.

You don't. When you're the one snoring.

Then the driving got strange.

I'd be coming back from a site visit in Coventry. I'd realise I'd been on the M6 for 20 minutes with no memory of the last three junctions. I'd been nodding off at the wheel.

I'd pull into services. Sit for 10 minutes. Two energy drinks. Carry on.

I still wake up exhausted every morning. My GP told me to persevere. That was 12 months ago.\n\nI need to tell you something I've been too embarrassed to say out loud.\n\nI'm 49. Married 22 years. Two kids. I'm a regional operations manager at a logistics firm in the West Midlands. Been there 14 years.\n\nTwelve months ago I was diagnosed with severe sleep apnoea. AHI of 47. I got a CPAP two months later.\n\nI have been using the machine every night since.\n\nMy AHI is 0.4. I wear the mask 8 hours a night. On paper the CPAP is working perfectly.\n\nI've done everything they told me to do.\n\nAnd I'm writing this at 3:14 AM because I woke up exhausted again - like I do every morning - and no doctor can help me.\n\nWho I Used To Be\n\nI used to be sharp.\n\nI remembered every customer. Every account number. Every quote I'd put in.\n\nI ran the Q3 review from memory. No notes. My deputy took notes.\n\nI coached Jack's football team until he was 14 and grew out of it.\n\nI fixed the boiler when it packed up in February. Fixed the neighbour's boiler the same week.\n\nI read to Sophie every night until she was 11.\n\nI was the man Claire married.\n\nI haven't been that man for about a year now.\n\nAnd here's the bit I still can't accept.\n\nThe CPAP didn't bring him back.\n\nWhat Started Happening Before The Diagnosis\n\nThe snoring got bad a couple of years ago. Claire told me. I didn't notice.\n\nYou don't. When you're the one snoring.\n\nThen the driving got strange.\n\nI'd be coming back from a site visit in Coventry. I'd realise I'd been on the M6 for 20 minutes with no memory of the last three junctions. I'd been nodding off at the wheel.\n\nI'd pull into services. Sit for 10 minutes. Two energy drinks. Carry on.\n\nI forgot the name of a client I'd been selling to for 11 years. Steve. Facilities director. He was sitting three feet from me in a meeting. I froze mid-sentence. Had to look at my notes.\n\nI came home that night. Sat in the car on the driveway for half an hour before I could go inside.\n\nMy dad had dementia. I watched him forget my mum's name. I was terrified I'd end up the same way.\n\nI finally went to my GP that April.\n\nThe Diagnosis And The Promise\n\nHome sleep study came back in June. AHI of 47. Severe apnoea.\n\nI stopped breathing 47 times an hour. Every hour. Every night.\n\nThe sleep clinic put me on the CPAP list. The machine came six weeks later. ResMed AirSense 11.\n\nThe specialist told me: \"You're going to feel like a new man in three months. Your energy will come back. Your memory will come back. The damage from years of untreated sleep apnoea reverses once we fix the AHI.\"\n\nI believed him.\n\nThe first two weeks were hard. Mask sizing. Seal issues. One night I ripped it off at 3 AM.\n\nThen I got the P30i cushion. Then it worked.\n\nBy month two my AHI was under 1. My snoring stopped. Claire slept.\n\nThe specialist said: \"You're doing everything right. Give it three months.\"\n\nI gave it three months.\n\nNothing changed.\n\nI went back to my specialist at month three. Told him I still felt exhausted every morning. Told him my head still felt full of cotton wool at work.\n\nHe looked at the numbers on his screen.\n\n\"Your AHI is 0.4, Andrew. The machine is doing its job. Sleep debt takes time to clear. Give it another three months.\"\n\nI gave it another three months.\n\nNothing changed.\n\nI went back at month six. Told him nothing had changed. He told me the same thing. Persevere. The CPAP is the gold standard. Give it time.\n\nI stopped going after that.\n\nAt month twelve I still woke up exhausted every morning. My head still felt full of cotton wool. And I hadn't been back to my specialist in half a year, because I already knew what he'd say.\n\nThe Number Says I'm Fixed. I'm Not.\n\nAHI: 0.4. Eight hours a night on the mask.\n\nPerfect numbers.\n\nI wake up at 4 AM most nights. Heart racing. No reason.\n\nI sit on the edge of the bed for two minutes before I can stand up.\n\nI can't remember words in meetings.\n\nI read the same email three times.\n\nI keep energy drinks in the cup holder. Pro Plus in the glove box. Claire doesn't know about the Pro Plus.\n\nLast Tuesday I sat down to help Jack with his GCSE maths. Simultaneous equations.
